I'd like to collect the currently known information on the strength of axiom-free Lean and how much classical math we should expect to be provable in it. My own research background is choiceless set theory, so I have a great interest in seeing what formal systems can handle without Choice, even though this isn't a priority for the mathlib community. I predict that down the road, there will be tools which can automatically convert substantial portions of mathlib into axiom-free counterparts, and those into Metamath's iset.mm library.

1) Lean admits axiom-free proofs of a syntactic translation of each theorem of Zermelo set theory (Z). This translation consists of the double negation translation of intuitionistic predicate calculus into classical, followed by quotienting out by extensional equivalence. This was developed by Harvey Friedman to show equiconsistency of IZF and ZF and also applies for translating Z into IZ, which is easily interpreted in CIC, and thus Lean. @Robin Arnez has formalized this translation.

Z is enough to interpret HOL proof systems, and its extension Z+KP is conservative with respect to provable validities of second-order logic (which encode virtually all mainstream mathematics). The main culprits of mainstream theorems to not admit a proof in Z are those which rely essentially on Choice, such as the Banach-Tarski paradox. (Contrary to popular belief, the bulk of classical measure theory can be reasonably carried out without Choice).

The strength of this theory can be pushed a bit further, e.g. Lean should be able to carry out Rathjen's type theoretic interpretation of Z+∃VΨ(ϵΩ+1)Z+\exists V_{\Psi(\epsilon_{\Omega+1})}Z+∃VΨ(ϵΩ+1​)​ (the ordinal is the Bachmann-Howard ordinal, a large computable ordinal).

2) Lean admits axiom-free proofs of every Π20\Pi^0_2Π20​ theorem of ZC+KP verbatim (see Friedman's technique for Π20\Pi^0_2Π20​-conservativity of LEM over nice intuitionistic theories, and my overview of Π41\Pi^1_4Π41​-conservativity of ZC+KP over Z). Π20\Pi^0_2Π20​ sentences are number theoretic propositions of the form "for all n, there exists m such that P(n, m)," where P is a computable property. Famous theorems at or below this complexity include:

  • FLT
  • PNT formulated with effective bounds
  • the weak Goldbach conjecture
  • infinitude of prime pairs of gap ≤246\le 246≤246
  • Baker's theorem restricted to computable reals
  • irrationality of ζ(3)\zeta(3)ζ(3)
  • CFSG
  • the quasi-polynomial time algorithm for Graph Isomorphism
  • PL Poincare conjecture in dimensions ≠4.\neq 4.=4.

Each of their proofs is known or expected to be formalizable in Z (e.g. see Colin McLarty's commentary on how to do this for FLT).

3) Every axiom-free theorem in Lean should be translatable to iset.mm (Metamath's intuitionistic set theory library) appended with a nested sequence of inaccessible sets. The iset.mm logical system is essentially equivalent to IZF set theory.  In Bruno Barras' habilitation thesis, page 135, he bounds the consistency strength of CIC below IZFR\mathrm{IZF}_{\mathrm{R}}IZFR​ + universes. Note that IZFR\mathrm{IZF}_{\mathrm{R}}IZFR​ is a subsystem of IZF (the former uses Replacement, which is weaker than Collection in intuitionistic settings).

Unfortunately, gauging the precise strength of CIC seems difficult. It is conjectured that ZF proves consistency of IZFR\mathrm{IZF}_{\mathrm{R}}IZFR​ (plus universes) but this has been open since Friedman's aforementioned work. Barras also discusses difficulties with achieving universe-by-universe equiconsistency of IZFR\mathrm{IZF}_{\mathrm{R}}IZFR​ vs CIC, in contrast to the success for classical CIC+AC vs ZFC with universes (see Werner's back-and-forth interpretations and @Mario Carneiro's analysis for Lean 3).

Also, until full verification of Lean is achieved, there is the risk that there are outstanding soundness bugs. A proof of False would not translate into Metamath, assuming set theory itself is consistent! But the vast majority of regularly used tactics presumably encode legitimate mathematical reasoning, so there is little reason to doubt that mathlib can be fully translated into set.mm and, with the above techniques formalized, mostly translated into iset.mm.

Huge thank you to @James E Hanson, @Loïc Pujet, @Jeremy Avigad, and Hanul Jeon for many helpful discussions as I compiled this information.

Just to check, when you say "axiom-free" do you mean "without any non-standard axioms" or also "without docs#Classical.choice" or even "without docs#Quot.sound or docs#propext" or worse yet "without the very restricted axiom-like behavior provided by CIC with inductive"?

Eric Wieser said:

Just to check, when you say "axiom-free" do you mean "without any non-standard axioms" or also "without docs#Classical.choice" or even "without docs#Quot.sound or docs#propext" or worse yet "without the very restricted axiom-like behavior provided by CIC with inductive"?

The middle of these. No Classical.choice, propext, or Quot.sound, but keeping the full underlying type theory. This is of course arbitrary accounting; Lean could have just as easily had more or fewer types baked into the kernel, but this gives us a clear base system to discuss.

this is very relevant to my interests! @Elliot Glazer i’m working on a linter tool & tentative graded scale for quantifying the oracle dependence for a given formulation in lean — ie how much classical machinery is actually needed for extraction vs verification.

C0-C5 scale defined here: https://github.com/brittlewis12/witness-budgets/blob/main/witness-budgets.md#11-the-c0c5-spectrum-grading-oracle-dependence

i’ve been exploring this extraction vs verification budget split to assess a few different constructive formulations i’ve worked on to demonstrate their utility. the early stages of this are available here: https://github.com/brittlewis12/witness-budgets

i’d love both feedback and to leverage this tool to map the degree of classical vs extractable formulations (and to hopefully inform & incentivize minimally axiomatic formulations!)

Interesting project! I'm having trouble distinguishing C0 vs C1 in the context of Lean. I'd think that distinction only makes sense for a system like Agda which is based on a predicative type theory. Would you say Lean's kernel is already at C1 level?

The non-linearity of the scale is a bit annoying but I agree these that roughly represent increasingly severe breaches of constructivity.

and your point on the nonlinearity is very fair, it's a somewhat arbitrary level system; perhaps a more coarse-grained approach would be sufficient? i figured up front more degrees of discrimination would go further, but so far those three tiers seem sufficient
This is super interesting to me. Look forward to seeing more.
Wouldn’t the lack of function extensionality (which is proven from quotient soundness in Lean) affect any potential result here, even starting at higher-order arithmetic?

The standard strategy to get around extensionality issues is to work with setoids (types equipped with an equivalence relation) instead of plain types, as one does in e.g. Bishop's constructive analysis. This way, it is possible to embed CIC + extensionality + quotient types in plain CIC.
Sure, the statements that one ends up writing are technically not the same as the statements one would write in Lean-with-axioms, but in the end, they encode the same mathematical results. And for first-order arithmetic statements, this makes no difference.

my working assumption has been that axiom-free lean has the same consistency strength as regular lean, as there are mechanisms to deal with most of the extensions using some combination of the proof that Con(ZFC) = Con(ZF), ett-to-itt, and homotopy canonicity results from hott

In my opinion, the real gap between CIC and Lean-with-axioms seems to revolve around unique choice (a.k.a function comprehension, or definite description), which tells you that functions are the same as functional relations. A naïve idea would be to systematically replace functions with functional relations, but this causes universe issues around Sigma-types and one cannot simulate replacement any more.

I strongly suspect that it is impossible to overcome this gap and that CIC is fundamentally weaker than IZF-with-replacement. Intuitively, without some form of unique choice, there is a strong separation between propositions and types (one could say that "the contents of the propositions cannot leak into types")
I'm not sure which of those systems you see as on which side of unique choice
lean-without-axioms doesn't have unique choice
Lean-with-axioms has unique choice (since it has full choice) but Lean-without-axioms does not have it
you think that the modeling of choice in ZF style would need unique choice?
Yes
it would be significant news if unique choice raised the consistency strength of lean-without-axioms
or CIC

I strongly expect that it is true, but I do not have a proof yet.
I've been trying on and off to put together a realisability model that makes this gap explicit, but there are lots of technicalities to sort out.

It seems to me that Otten and Van den Berg's model is concerned with a pretty weak type theory, where natural numbers cannot be eliminated into large types. So you cannot define e.g. Σ(n:N) . Pn(N)\Sigma (n : N)~.~\mathcal{P}^n(\mathbb{N})Σ(n:N) . Pn(N) and all the crazy types that come from large elimination + Sigma and Pi

@Cameron Zwarich as far as I understand, the correct analogue to the double negation translation in presence of types with computational content (such as natural numbers) is double negation sheaves -- similar to what's described in the paper of Rijke Shulman and Spitters on modalities in HoTT : https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.07526

Their setting assumes propositional resizing and some beefy higher inductive types, I don't really know if we can replicate it with an impredicative sort and setoids. Would be interesting to look into...

I might be misreading something, but do they mention this somewhere in their paper? They consider an assembly model in their paper, and such models support natural numbers that allow one to eliminate in any type (see the elimination rule in Section 3 of the arxiv version, the published version has printing errors). One needs to be careful in the construction (see the discussion in Section 3.1), but the construction they give in Appendix B should give large elimination.

As far as I can tell, they have a universe Set (interpreted as modest assemblies/PER) and they can do elimination of natural numbers into Set. But Prop is not in set itself, so they can't use their type theory to define "large" types such as Σ(n:N) . Pn(N)\Sigma (n : N)~.~\mathcal{P}^n(\mathbb{N})Σ(n:N) . Pn(N) (where P\mathcal{P}P is interpreted as functions into Prop)

And indeed, if they could define this type I'm talking about, they would have a problem, since this type can be used to build a model of higher-order arithmetic!

I'm not sure I agree with your analysis of their model. They are unfortunately somewhat vague about the details of their type theory, but I think they do allow things like your set. They claim that this works because the powersets of the CIC are not full, they use something like computable functions only

Functions Nat -> Bool are somewhat tame indeed. But functions Nat -> Prop are much more difficult to interpret! If you look at their model construction, they interpret Prop as ∇Subsing, a codiscrete assembly. Thus any term tracks any function from Nat to ∇Subsing, and there are uncountably many such functions.
Repeat that argument for higher types, and you get that their interpretation of (Nat -> Prop) -> Prop is roughly the double powerset of the integers, etc. Since their metatheory only supplies them with a finite amount of powersets, they cannot collect all of these together in their model.
so is it allowed to construct functions into Type by recursion on Nat?
IIUC they allow constructing functions into Set, and also Prop

As you said, they are a bit vague with their theory unfortunately
But they have to either forbid large elimination from Nat to Type, or Sigma-types whose codomain is in Type

While I'm at it, here are some basic observations that might help estimate the strength of CIC:

  • There seems to be some sense in which N→Prop\mathbb{N} \to \mathsf{Prop}N→Prop requires an uncountable set in set-theoretic models. After all, one can build a model of second-order Heyting arithmetic in type theory whose carrier type is N→Prop\mathbb{N} \to \mathsf{Prop}N→Prop, and I'm pretty sure that set theory without powerset is weaker than second-order arithmetic.
  • Likewise, there is some sense in which (N→Prop)→Prop(\mathbb{N} \to \mathsf{Prop}) \to \mathsf{Prop}(N→Prop)→Prop seems to require the second powerset of N\mathbb{N}N in models
  • Extending this pattern, it seems that Pn(N)\mathcal{P}^n(\mathbb{N})Pn(N) requires nnn powersets from the metatheory
  • We can go up fairly high in the cardinal hierarchy if we trust this intuition: Σ(n:N).Pn(N)\Sigma(n : \mathbb{N}).\mathcal{P}^n(\mathbb{N})Σ(n:N).Pn(N) would be comparable to ℶω\beth_\omegaℶω​, and by iterating this construction, we quickly get ℶω⋅ω\beth_{\omega \cdot \omega}ℶω⋅ω​, then ℶωω\beth_{\omega^\omega}ℶωω​, then ℶϵ0\beth_{\epsilon_0}ℶϵ0​​, etc.
  • If we have large elimination for the accessibility predicate (as we do in CIC), we can iterate these type-theoretic powersets along any well-founded order. Given a type A:TypeA : \mathsf{Type}A:Type, a relation R:A→A→PropR : A \to A \to \mathsf{Prop}R:A→A→Prop and an element a:Aa : Aa:A which is accessible, we can define ℶa\beth_aℶa​ which iterates powerset along all the predecessors of aaa. Then, we can use a sigma-type to take the sup of these types across all accessible relations on N\mathbb{N}N, which seems to be a good type-theoretic analogue to ℶω1\beth_{\omega_1}ℶω1​​.

So, CIC seems very strong! But somehow, maybe not quite up to par with ZFC.

No, CIC proves the existence of Vω1V_{\omega_1}Vω1​​ using 2 universes using a more elaborate version of Loic's counterexample:

/-- Countable well-founded relations, as a *small* type. Uses Prop : Type. -/
def WO : Type := { R : Nat → Nat → Prop // WellFounded R }

/-- The stage function along R: T R n is the powerset of the disjoint union
    of all earlier stages. Well-founded recursion with a Type-valued motive,
    i.e. Acc large elimination into Type; the motive `fun _ => Type` lives in
    Nat → Type 1, so this needs Type : Type 1. -/
def T (R : Nat → Nat → Prop) (h : WellFounded R) : Nat → Type :=
  h.fix fun n ih => (Σ' m : Nat, Σ' hm : R m n, ih m hm) → Prop

/-- One small type containing a stage for every countable ordinal. -/
def V₁ : Type := Σ w : WO, Σ n : Nat, T w.1 w.2 n

/-
Sanity check for Definition "the materializing recursion" (paper3, section
"Accessibility on a big carrier gives Replacement"): the recursion typechecks in
Lean 4 core, axiom-free, with carrier and motive both `PSet.{u} : Type (u+1)`.
Only the definition and its unfolding equation are here; `D` stands for
"well-orderings of subsets of G ∪ ω" and is left abstract. Lemma mat is not formalized.
-/
universe u

inductive PSet : Type (u+1)
  | mk (α : Type u) (A : α → PSet) : PSet

namespace PSet
def Idx : PSet.{u} → Type u | ⟨α, _⟩ => α
def Func : (x : PSet.{u}) → x.Idx → PSet.{u} | ⟨_, A⟩ => A

def empty : PSet.{u} := ⟨PEmpty, PEmpty.elim⟩
def sUnion (a : PSet.{u}) : PSet.{u} :=
  ⟨Σ x : a.Idx, (a.Func x).Idx, fun ⟨x, y⟩ => (a.Func x).Func y⟩
def pair2 (a b : PSet.{u}) : PSet.{u} := ⟨ULift Bool, fun i => if i.down then a else b⟩
def sing (a : PSet.{u}) : PSet.{u} := pair2 a a
def succ (x : PSet.{u}) : PSet.{u} := sUnion (pair2 x (sing x))
def pr (a b : PSet.{u}) : PSet.{u} := pair2 (sing a) (pair2 a b)
/-- `{t | P}`: a set guarded by a proposition. -/
def guard (P : Prop) (t : P → PSet.{u}) : PSet.{u} :=
  ⟨ULift.{u} (PLift P), fun h => t h.down.down⟩
def tag (n s : PSet.{u}) : PSet.{u} := ⟨s.Idx, fun i => pr n (s.Func i)⟩
def one : PSet.{u} := sing empty
def two : PSet.{u} := succ one

variable (D : PSet.{u} → PSet.{u}) (uu : PSet.{u})

def labels (G : PSet.{u}) : PSet.{u} :=
  sUnion (pair2 (sing empty) (sUnion (pair2 (sing (tag one (D G))) (sing (tag two uu)))))

def step (R : PSet.{u} → PSet.{u} → Prop) (p : PSet.{u})
    (rec : (c : PSet.{u}) → R c p → PSet.{u}) : PSet.{u} :=
  let G := sUnion (guard (R (pr p empty) p) (fun h => rec (pr p empty) h))
  sUnion ⟨(labels D uu G).Idx, fun i =>
    let v := (labels D uu G).Func i
    sUnion (guard (R (pr p v) p) fun h => succ (rec (pr p v) h))⟩

def F (R : PSet.{u} → PSet.{u} → Prop) (p : PSet.{u}) (a : Acc R p) : PSet.{u} :=
  Acc.rec (motive := fun _ _ => PSet.{u}) (fun p _ ih => step D uu R p ih) a

theorem F_eq (R) (p : PSet.{u}) (a : Acc R p) :
    F D uu R p a = step D uu R p (fun c h => F D uu R c (a.inv h)) := by
  cases a; rfl

Yes, the same story goes for a theory with precisely nnn universes (and without accessibility). In set theoretic terms, my model basically

  • Starts by normalising the predicative part of the theory (which is MLTT with W-types and as many universes as CIC has) by associating a countable ordinal to each type in normal form. Since we are only caring about the predicative part here (by erasing propositions), this can be done with very little strength from the meta theory
  • From this, one obtains an ordinal bound on the "complexity" of every type
  • Then I build a second model which does not erase proofs, to get consistency. In that model, every type is interpreted as an assembly whose rank is bounded by the corresponding ordinal. This is where I will need that V_alpha exist for all of these ordinals
It's important that I don't have accessibility in the theory, because in presence of accessibility it is not possible to decorrelate the predicative layer from the impredicative layer to this extent

/-- The relation of a target assignment: `c` is a child of `p` and has a target. -/
def Rel (τ : Path.{u} → PSet.{u} → Prop) (c p : Path.{u}) : Prop :=
  ∃ l, c = l :: p ∧ ∃ t, τ c t

/-- `G` is the target of the child `a` of `p`, or empty if there is none. -/
def IsG (τ : Path.{u} → PSet.{u} → Prop) (p : Path.{u}) (G : PSet.{u}) : Prop :=
  ∀ x, x ∈ G ↔ ∃ ζ, τ (.a :: p) ζ ∧ x ∈ ζ

/-- The labels the step enumerates when the first call returns `G`. -/
def Avail (G : PSet.{u}) (l : Label.{u}) : Prop :=
  l = .a ∨ (∃ w, w ∈ D G ∧ l.Equiv (.b w)) ∨ ∃ x, x ∈ U ∧ l.Equiv (.c x)

/-- A coherent target assignment. It is a proposition about a relation; no part of it is
data. -/
structure Coherent (τ : Path.{u} → PSet.{u} → Prop) : Prop where
  /-- targets are determined up to bisimulation -/
  resp : ∀ {p t t'}, τ p t → t ≈ t' → τ p t'
  func : ∀ {p t t'}, τ p t → τ p t' → t ≈ t'
  /-- the assignment does not see the representation of a label -/
  lab : ∀ {l l' p t}, Label.Equiv l l' → τ (l :: p) t → τ (l' :: p) t
  /-- the target of a child is an element of the target of its parent -/
  desc : ∀ {l p t t'}, τ (l :: p) t → τ p t' → t ∈ t'
  /-- a target is the union of the successors of the targets of the available children -/
  sup : ∀ {p t G}, τ p t → IsG τ p G →
    ∀ x, x ∈ t ↔ ∃ l t', Avail D U G l ∧ τ (l :: p) t' ∧ x ∈ succ t'

variable {T s φ} {C : PSet.{u} → Prop}
  (hT : ∀ η, C η → Coherent D s (T η) ∧ T η [] η)
  (hTresp : ∀ {η η' p t}, η ≈ η' → T η p t → T η' p t)
  (φ_resp : ∀ {x x' y y'}, x ≈ x' → y ≈ y' → φ x y → φ x' y')
  (φ_func : ∀ {x y y'}, x ∈ s → φ x y → φ x y' → y ≈ y')
  (φ_C : ∀ {x y}, x ∈ s → φ x y → C y)

/-- **Replacement** for `φ` on `s`, provided the values of `φ` lie in a class `C` every member
`η` of which is the root target of a coherent assignment `T η` given uniformly in `η`. -/
theorem replacement : ∃ img : PSet.{u}, ∀ y, y ∈ img ↔ ∃ x, x ∈ s ∧ φ x y := by
  have ⟨θ, hθ⟩ := exists_sup hT hTresp φ_resp φ_func φ_C
  refine ⟨sep (fun y => ∃ x, x ∈ s ∧ φ x y) θ, fun y => ?_⟩
  rw [mem_sep fun y y' e ⟨x, hx, h⟩ => ⟨x, hx, φ_resp (Equiv.refl _) e h⟩]
  refine ⟨fun h => h.2, fun ⟨x, hx, h⟩ => ⟨(hθ y).2 ⟨x, y, hx, h, ?_⟩, x, hx, h⟩⟩
  exact mem_succ.2 (.inr (Equiv.refl _))

class Stable (p : Prop) : Prop where
  dne : ¬¬p → p

/-- `p` is in the well-founded part of `R` as far as stable predicates can tell. -/
def SWF {α : Sort _} (R : α → α → Prop) (p : α) : Prop :=
  ∀ P : α → Prop, (∀ x, Stable (P x)) → (∀ x, (∀ y, R y x → P y) → P x) → P p

/-- Labels of children: the child `a`, whose value `G` is computed first; the children
`b w` for `w ∈ D G`; and the children `c x` for `x` in a parameter set. -/
inductive Label : Type (u+1)
  | a
  | b (w : PSet.{u})
  | c (x : PSet.{u})

/-- A path, deepest label first. The carrier of the recursion; it lives in `Type (u+1)`,
the same universe as `PSet.{u}`. -/
abbrev Path := List Label.{u}

/-- The one hypothesis: a root that is well-founded for stable predicates is not not
accessible. It follows from the irrefutability of excluded middle. -/
def AccHyp : Prop :=
  ∀ R : Path.{u} → Path.{u} → Prop, SWF R [] → ¬¬Acc R []

/-- The accessibility hypothesis follows from the irrefutability of excluded middle. -/
theorem accHyp_of_not_not_em (h : ¬¬∀ p : Prop, p ∨ ¬p) : AccHyp.{u} := fun R swf hn =>
  h fun em => hn <| swf (fun p => Acc R p)
    (fun p => ⟨fun hp => (em (Acc R p)).resolve_right hp⟩) fun x ih => ⟨x, ih⟩

/-- **The consistency of `ZF`**, from the accessibility hypothesis alone. -/
theorem con_ZF (hacc : AccHyp.{0}) : Con ZF := (hg_model hacc).con

"Definitional Proof Irrelevance Made Accessible" provides a type theory with an impredicative (definitionally) proof-irrelevant universe (like Lean's Prop), an infinite predicative hierarchy of proof-relevant universes (like Lean's Type us), and a Acc which lives in Prop and has large-elimination, as well as a proof of soundness of that system

@Talia Ringer In the "standard" definition of CIC (both implemented by Rocq and Lean, although Lean takes some liberties), large elimination of inductive propositions is generally disallowed. But there is one exception, called the subsingleton criterion. If your inductive proposition

  • has at most one constructor
  • has all the arguments of said constructor being propositions

Then large elimination is allowed. There are three important propositions which satisfy that criterion

  • The False proposition. Large elim of False allows you to prune impossible branches, even though the proof of impossibility lives in Prop
  • Martin-Löf's inductive equality. Large elim of eq allows you to do transport in types, even though the equality lives in Prop
  • The accessibility predicate. Large elim of acc allows you to do well-founded recursion to define stuff in Type, even though the proof of well-foundedness lives in Prop
Large elimination for these is allowed by Rocq and Lean, and is consistent (it is validated by the usual model in ZFC + inaccessibles)
